passage: Snack-time note, Wednesday. Damini pointed toward the biscuit tin and said something short that I heard as "nana," so I brought a banana. Damini pushed it away, cried, and sat with arms folded, refusing the banana and everything else I offered. The snack was late and Damini stayed hungry. I could not tell what was wanted because nothing clear was said. Next time I will hold up both foods and ask which one. Hemant

qa.q: What did Damini push away?
qa.a: Damini pushed away the banana.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when the banana was offered?
qa.a: Damini was disappointed and angry, because Damini had wanted the biscuit and the banana was the wrong thing.

qa.q: What other approach could work for Damini, and why?
qa.a: Damini could point at the tin and say "biscuit" while walking to Hemant, because clearer words and a shown target make it easier for an adult to get it right.

qa.q: How does Hemant see what went wrong?
qa.a: Hemant heard a short unclear word and guessed, and now sees that holding up both foods and asking is a better plan.

grounding: A toddler who wanted a biscuit is offered a banana, pushes it away and cries, because the goal was fixed on one thing and the request was not clear.

passage: On the verandah of the kasba house Manoj wailed for a biscuit. Uday, Manoj's father, held out a banana instead and waited. Manoj cried harder, then sniffed, went quiet and looked at the banana for a long moment. Both small hands reached out, took it and pushed it toward the mouth. Uday peeled the top for Manoj and said nothing at all. 😊

qa.q: What did Uday hold out instead of a biscuit?
qa.a: Uday held out a banana.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling while crying for the biscuit, and what changed?
qa.a: Manoj was sad and disappointed, but hunger and a long look at the banana shifted Manoj toward accepting it.

qa.q: What could Manoj try next time to get the food wanted, and why?
qa.a: Manoj could say "biscuit, please" and point at the tin before crying, because asking clearly gives Uday a chance to choose.

qa.q: How does Uday see the moment Manoj takes the banana?
qa.a: Uday is relieved and quietly pleased that Manoj took some food, and stays silent so that the choice remains Manoj's.

grounding: After crying for a biscuit, a toddler sniffs, looks at the banana and takes it, changing the plan from a specific food to some food.

passage: Nitin sat on the flat's living room floor and piled up wooden blocks, one on another: one, two, three, four, five, six. At the sixth the tower toppled with a clatter. Farhan, Nitin's older cousin, looked up from his book. Nitin did not cry or complain, only said "Again," and built it once more, this time with the long block first and the small ones later. It grew to seven before it fell.

qa.q: How many blocks were in the tower when it fell the first time?
qa.a: The tower fell when the sixth block went on.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling after the tower toppled?
qa.a: Nitin was calm and determined, since there was no crying and only "Again," and the rebuild started right away.

qa.q: What alternative approach could help Nitin build higher, and why?
qa.a: Nitin could ask Farhan how he would stack the blocks, or make the bottom wider, because a small change to the base can matter more than luck.

qa.q: How might Farhan see Nitin's way of building?
qa.a: Farhan sees a patient child trying a new order each time; he keeps reading instead of stepping in, which suggests he trusts Nitin to work it out.

grounding: A child stacks blocks into a tower, watches it fall at the sixth, and builds again with the blocks in a slightly different order.

passage: "Five minutes till dinner," Nilesh called from the kitchen, and rain drummed on the window. Vasudha knelt by the blocks and muttered, "Big ones down. Then the little ones. Then the flag." She lined up the big blocks side by side, set the small ones on top, and pushed the paper flag into the last block. The tower stood tall and even. Nilesh peeked in and whistled.

qa.q: What did Vasudha put on top of the tower?
qa.a: Vasudha pushed the paper flag into the last block on top.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling as she muttered the order of blocks?
qa.a: Vasudha was focused and confident, because she had a plan and wanted to finish before dinner.

qa.q: What alternative could Vasudha use if the tower starts to wobble, and why?
qa.a: She could widen the bottom or ask Nilesh to steady it, because a step list keeps the order, but a wobble asks for a change to the base.

qa.q: How does Nilesh see Vasudha's tower?
qa.a: Nilesh, who peeked in and whistled, is impressed at how tall and even the tower is, since Vasudha finished it in a few minutes.

grounding: A child tells herself the order in which to build, big blocks then small then a flag, and the list keeps the tower's shape in mind as it grows.

passage: The community hall was loud with a birthday party, and Uday sat on the mat with a bucket of blocks, frowning at his fallen towers. Then he noticed Rukmini, the neighbour, at the next mat, laying two long blocks side by side before adding more. Uday copied it, base first. His tower rose past every one he had built before. "It just stays up," he said, puzzled, and grinned.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do with the two long blocks?
qa.a: Rukmini laid two long blocks side by side before adding more.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when the tower rose past his earlier ones?
qa.a: Uday was pleased and a bit puzzled, since he grinned but could only say "It just stays up."

qa.q: What alternative could help Uday, and why?
qa.a: Uday could ask Rukmini why the base matters or test a wide and a narrow base himself, because understanding the reason would help him build well with any blocks.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see Uday copying the base?
qa.a: Rukmini may not have noticed at all in a loud hall, or may be flattered; either way the base works and Uday's tower is proof.

grounding: A boy copies a neighbour's wide base of two long blocks and builds higher than before without being able to explain why.

passage: "Stay up, tower!" Selin whispered, and set the red block on top. "Red is lucky." The tower, built on two small blocks, wobbled and crashed. "Bad red block!" Selin cried and threw it under the table. Sami, Selin's older brother, gathered the rest. The next tower began on the same two small blocks, red block on top, and it fell again, faster.

qa.q: Where did Selin put the lucky red block?
qa.a: Selin set the red block on top of the tower.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling when the tower crashed?
qa.a: Selin was upset and angry at the red block, blaming the block instead of the tower's base.

qa.q: What alternative approach could work for Selin, and why?
qa.a: Selin could try a wider base of bigger blocks before adding the red one, because a firm base is what keeps a tower up and luck cannot change that.

qa.q: How does Sami see the second fall?
qa.a: Sami has probably noticed that the base stayed the same and the tower fell again, so he keeps picking up blocks, maybe unsure how to say it kindly.

grounding: A child says "stay up" to a tower and trusts a lucky block, then blames the block rather than the narrow base when the tower wobbles.

passage: Only ten blocks were left before Sunaina, the teacher, rang the tidy-up bell. Pranav had built three towers and watched each one fall. Pranav sat back, thought, and said aloud, "If it wobbles, make the bottom wider." The fourth tower began with four blocks side by side. It leaned a little, so Pranav slid in a fifth beside them. That tower stayed standing when the bell rang.

qa.q: How many blocks were left before the tidy-up bell?
qa.a: Ten blocks were left before Sunaina rang the tidy-up bell.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling after three towers had fallen?
qa.a: Pranav was thoughtful and a little frustrated, which led to sitting back and making a rule aloud.

qa.q: What else could Pranav try if the tower still wobbles, and why?
qa.a: Pranav could add a wider base and put the small blocks on the top, because a tower of heavy blocks low down is steadier.

qa.q: How does Sunaina see the tower standing when the bell rang?
qa.a: Sunaina, who is ringing the bell for tidy-up, sees a child who used a rule and is likely to be pleased that the fourth tower stood.

grounding: After three collapses a child decides that if it wobbles the bottom should be wider and uses that rule on the next tower, replacing guessing with a tested rule.

passage:
"Whoa, it fell again," said Farhan.
"I hate this!" Arohi swept an arm across the mat and sent every block skidding.
"Hey, my foot!"
"Stupid tower!" Arohi's voice cracked.
"You got it up to six last time."
"Don't care." Arohi crossed both arms and stared at the wall.
Farhan sighed, Arohi's big brother, and began collecting the blocks.

qa.q: What did Arohi do with the blocks after the tower fell?
qa.a: Arohi swept an arm across the mat and sent every block skidding.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when saying "I hate this"?
qa.a: Arohi was angry and disappointed, with a cracking voice that shows the feeling was bigger than the block problem.

qa.q: What could Arohi try after calming down, and why?
qa.a: Arohi could rebuild with a wider base of the long blocks, because the earlier tries had shown what nearly worked, and calm helps to use it.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Arohi's outburst?
qa.a: Farhan is a bit surprised and hurt by the flying blocks, but he stays patient and begins to tidy up rather than scold.

grounding: When the tower falls a fourth time, a child sweeps the blocks off the mat and says "I hate this," so feelings run ahead of thinking.

passage: I was on the sofa when Disha asked her father, "Papa, hold this one?" He kept a hand steady on the lowest block as she piled. Then she stopped stacking and watched how he turned each block until its edges lined up square. Later, alone, she set every block down that way and her tower rose straighter than before. I cannot tell what Disha thought, but she certainly watched closely. Vaibhav

qa.q: What did Disha ask her father to do?
qa.a: Disha asked her father, "Papa, hold this one?"

qa.q: What might Disha have been feeling while watching her father line up the blocks?
qa.a: Disha was probably curious and attentive, since she stopped stacking to watch, though Vaibhav says that thinking cannot be seen.

qa.q: What else could Disha try if her tower still leans, and why?
qa.a: Disha could also make the bottom wider or check that each block is square before adding the next, because a square, wide base gives a firmer tower.

qa.q: How might Disha's father see her asking for help?
qa.a: Her father likely feels glad to be asked; he is happy to hold the block and lets Disha stack, which fits a parent who wants to help without taking over.

grounding: A child asks her father to hold the bottom block while she stacks, watches how he sets the blocks square, and copies that placement when building alone.

passage: Right at the centre of the living room, Tejas squeezed both eyes shut, pressed both hands over them and stood very still. Jasleen, Tejas's older cousin, finished counting and turned round. "Found you!" Jasleen laughed. Tejas uncovered and looked stunned. "But I could not see you!" The round was over almost before it began, and Tejas's lip trembled.

qa.q: Where did Tejas stand while covering both eyes?
qa.a: Tejas stood at the centre of the living room.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when Jasleen said "Found you!"?
qa.a: Tejas was stunned and upset, because Tejas believed that not seeing meant not being seen, which is why the lip trembled.

qa.q: What alternative could Tejas try next round, and why?
qa.a: Tejas could run behind the sofa or a curtain while Jasleen counts, because hiding needs a place where the seeker cannot see.

qa.q: How does Jasleen see Tejas standing with hands over the eyes?
qa.a: Jasleen sees the child in plain view and laughs at the easy find, likely not realising how upset Tejas will be.

grounding: A four-year-old covers both eyes in the middle of the room and believes nobody can see, unable to take the seeker's point of view.
